content: Umbilical cord blood is a type of human blood that is collected from the placenta and umbilical cord after the umbilical cord has been detached from a newborn. This blood is a rich source of hematopoietic stem cells, which are used in stem cell transplantation. Cord blood can be stored in either public or private cord blood banks. Public cord blood banks store donated cord blood for the benefit of the general public, often coordinating with the National Marrow Donor Program (NMDP) in the United States to match cord blood units to patients in need. In contrast, private cord blood banks are for-profit organizations that store cord blood exclusively for the donor or their family members. The medical community strongly supports public cord blood banking, while private cord blood banking is generally discouraged unless there is a family history of specific genetic diseases. In some countries, such as France and Italy, private cord blood banking is illegal and opposed by ethical organizations like the European Group on Ethics in Science and New Technologies. Cord blood stem cells are highly proliferative and have a greater likelihood of matching family members compared to stem cells derived from bone marrow. Parents and siblings share 50% of the genetic markers of the donor’s stem cells, but achieving a full match requires compatibility across many genetic markers, making the probability of a successful match lower. Additional stem cells can also be collected from the placenta through a process called Placenta Cord Banking. After the healthcare provider collects cord blood from the umbilical cord, the placenta is sent to a laboratory for further processing to extract additional stem cells. By banking both placental and umbilical cord blood stem cells, families can potentially store up to twice the number of CD34+ stem cells, which are critical for successful transplants. Research has shown that the number of CD34+ cells in a transplant is a key factor in treatment success and patient survival. Cord blood can be collected using two methods: in utero (before the placenta is delivered) or ex utero (after the placenta is delivered). In the ex utero method, the umbilical cord is clamped after the baby is delivered, and the placenta is placed in a sterile structure to allow blood to drain by gravity, yielding 40–150 mL of cord blood. In the in utero method, the cord blood is collected after the baby is delivered but before the placenta is expelled. Once collected, the cord blood is immediately sent to a cord blood bank for processing. At public cord blood banks, the blood is tested for infectious agents, tissue-typed, and processed to remove red blood cells before being cryopreserved in liquid nitrogen for future use. New parents can choose to store their newborn’s cord blood in a private bank or donate it to a public bank. Private cord blood banking costs approximately $2,000 for collection and $125 per year for storage (as of 2007). Public donation is free for the donor, although some obstetricians may charge a collection fee. Public donation options are expanding, with more local cord blood banks in the United States accepting donations. The first sibling-donor cord blood transplant was performed in 1988, and the National Institutes of Health (NIH) later funded the establishment of the world’s first cord blood program at the New York Blood Center to create an inventory of unrelated, matched stem cell units for transplantation. In 2005, a method was developed at the University of Toronto to increase the yield of cord blood stem cells, enabling their use in treating adults as well as children. When cryopreserved cord blood is needed for treatment, it is thawed, washed to remove the cryoprotectant, and administered to the patient via intravenous injection. If the stem cells are collected from a donor, the treatment is referred to as allogeneic. If the cells are collected from the same individual who will receive the treatment, it is called autologous. When the cells are collected from genetically identical individuals, it is termed syngeneic. Xenogeneic transfer, involving cells from different species, is still in its infancy and has limited research potential. The medical community generally supports public cord blood banking, but private banking has been met with criticism from governments and nonprofit organizations. The controversy stems from differing opinions on the likelihood of stored cord blood being used successfully in the future. Estimates of the probability that a child will require an autologous stem cell transplant by age 20 vary widely, with proponents citing odds of 1 in 2,700 and critics citing odds as low as 1 in 20,000. The European Union Group on Ethics has questioned the legitimacy of private cord blood banks, arguing that they sell a service with no proven therapeutic value and make promises they cannot fulfill. The World Marrow Donor Association has also stated that autologous cord blood is not suitable for treating childhood leukemia due to the presence of pre-leukemic cells at birth and that it carries the same genetic defects as the donor, making it unsuitable for treating genetic diseases. Currently, there are no established protocols for using autologous cord blood in therapy, and future protocols are expected to rely on more accessible stem cell sources. Since the late 1980s, cord blood stem cells have been used to treat various blood and immune system-related genetic diseases, cancers, and disorders. However, due to medical concerns about using one’s own cells, most treatments involve stem cells from unrelated donors. In 1993, Dr. Joanne Kurtzberg performed the first two successful unrelated donor cord blood transplants, one of which cured acute lymphoblastic leukemia. A comprehensive list of diseases treated with cord blood can be found on the National Marrow Donor Program website. In 2005, U.S. Representative Chris Smith introduced the “Stem Cell Therapeutic and Research Act of 2005,” which allocated $265 million to support stem cell therapy, umbilical cord blood, and bone marrow treatments. The law aimed to expand the nation’s public cord blood inventory by adding 150,000 new units and creating a genetically diverse collection to match 90% of patients in need. It also established a national registry to facilitate the search for cord blood and bone marrow matches. The National Marrow Donor Program (NMDP) was selected to oversee these efforts. The law also mandated that cord blood deemed unsuitable for transplantation be donated for research purposes, further advancing the field of cord blood stem cell research.
